What the website can show

Recognition, decision-making, and communication choices in a scenario. A screen can check those.

What only an instructor can verify

Physical performance on a task trainer. That takes training equipment and a qualified observer with an approved checklist. The lesson assigns that part to the instructor.

Built on learning theory

Objectives are written to Bloom's taxonomy, practice follows adult learning principles, and the lesson is evaluated with Kirkpatrick's four levels.

How this lesson is built

Experience the Lesson

Lesson Overview

Uncontrolled bleeding can become life-threatening within minutes. This lesson prepares the learner to recognize it, control it with direct pressure, and hand the casualty off with a clear report.

Terminal learning objective

Given a simulated external-bleeding casualty, a task trainer, a training first-aid kit, and a second responder, the learner will control bleeding with direct pressure and deliver a verbal handoff, performing all critical steps on the performance checklist without instructor prompting.

Enabling learning objectives

By the end of this lesson, the learner will:

  1. Identify the signs of life-threatening external bleeding in a given scenario.
  2. Select the correct initial safety and help-activation actions.
  3. Apply and maintain direct pressure on a task trainer in accordance with the performance checklist.
  4. Reassess bleeding and take corrective action when bleeding continues.
  5. Deliver a verbal handoff that states the injury, the actions taken, and the casualty's current status.

How the lesson runs

  • Online, 5 to 7 minutes. Scenario, response sequence, and a three-question knowledge check.
  • Practical, 23 minutes. Instructor demonstration, guided practice on a task trainer, and an individual performance assessment.

Experience the Lesson

Scenario

Field training exercise, day three

It is 0540 and still half dark. Your squad is breaking down the tent line when a metal stake clatters on the gravel and Reyes shouts.

He is a few feet away, gripping his forearm. Blood runs between his fingers and drips off his elbow. He looks straight at you. "It won't stop."

Carter drops her pack beside you. The aid bag is ten feet away. The area is clear and nobody else is hurt.

Experience the Lesson

The Response Sequence

The initial response has four parts. Learn them in order.

  1. RecognizeConfirm the scene is safe and put on gloves. Look at how much blood there is and how it is moving. Blood that flows continuously or spurts is life-threatening. So is blood loss equal to about half a soda can.
  2. RespondDirect one specific person to call for emergency help and bring the kit. Find the source of the bleeding. Place a dressing on the wound and apply steady, firm pressure directly over it. Keep the injured limb on a firm, flat surface.
  3. ReassessHold pressure until the bleeding stops or you are relieved. If blood soaks through, leave the first dressing in place and add a gauze pad on top. If bleeding continues, keep the pressure on and call for more help.
  4. ReportWhen help arrives, state the injury, the actions you took, and the casualty's current status. Stay with the casualty until you are relieved.

Recognition check: which one is the emergency?

Recognize is the first step, and it is a judgment call. Most injuries that bleed are minor. A few will kill someone in minutes. Two people get hurt at the same neighborhood pool, an hour apart. Read both cases, then make the call.

Case 1: The scraped palm

Your nephew runs on the wet deck, slips, and lands on his hands. He holds up a scraped palm and starts to cry. A little blood wells up slowly. You press a towel on it, and a minute later the towel has one small spot.

Case 2: The broken tile

A man climbing out of the pool drags his forearm across a broken tile edge. Blood runs down to his wrist in a steady stream. He grabs a towel, and it is red in seconds. His daughter is standing behind him, watching.

Back to Reyes

Both of your hands are on the dressing. Reyes keeps asking if it is bad. Then you feel warmth spreading under your palms. The gauze is soaked and blood is still coming. Carter is on the radio with her back to you.

Content source: American Red Cross, Bleeding, Life-Threatening External. See Sources.

Experience the Lesson

Hands-On Practice

The practical portion takes place in the classroom with an instructor and a task trainer. It has three stages.

  1. DemonstrationThe instructor performs the full skill once at normal speed, then again step by step while explaining each decision.
  2. Guided practiceThe learner practices on the task trainer with a partner. The instructor gives specific corrective feedback and introduces a "bleeding continues" cue.
  3. Individual assessmentThe learner performs the full sequence alone, without coaching, while the instructor scores each step on the performance checklist.

Equipment

  • Simulated limb or bleeding-control task trainer
  • Training dressings and gauze
  • Gloves
  • Scenario cards
  • Performance checklist

Standard

The learner must perform every critical step on the checklist without prompting. A learner who is prompted on a critical step, or misses one, receives targeted remediation and a second attempt.

View the performance checklist

Knowledge Check

Answer all three questions, then select Submit answers. Your first submission is recorded as your initial score. You can then review and correct any missed item.

Experience the Lesson

Lesson Summary

Next step: practical assessment

The online portion is complete. The learner now moves to supervised practice and an individual, instructor-observed performance assessment on the task trainer. Physical performance is assessed in person.

Review the Design | Section A

Design brief

This lesson was built to show a complete design process for a performance-based task: measurable objectives, aligned instruction, decision practice, instructor-observed assessment, remediation, and evaluation.

Task

Control external bleeding with direct pressure and hand the casualty off to arriving help.

Training need

Learners can often recall the steps of an emergency response and still struggle to organize their actions, perform the physical skill, or communicate what they have done. The lesson therefore assesses knowledge and decisions online, and physical performance in person.

Audience, delivery, and scope
ElementSpecification
Target audienceEntry-level medical trainees who have completed instruction in scene safety, standard precautions, and emergency activation
Training settingControlled, non-tactical simulation environment
Online component5 to 7 minutes
Practical component23 minutes, with added time or staffing as group size requires
EquipmentSimulated limb or bleeding-control task trainer, training dressings, gloves, scenario cards, and a performance checklist
In scopeRecognition, initial response decisions, direct pressure, reassessment, requesting assistance, and handoff communication
Follow-on lessonsTourniquet application, wound packing, CPR, tactical casualty care, and comprehensive patient assessment

Validation before fielding

As with any new lesson, three steps come before it reaches a classroom:

  1. A medical subject-matter expert reviews the clinical content and the checklist's critical steps.
  2. METC confirms the task, prerequisites, equipment, and time available.
  3. A small pilot tests the materials, the timing, and assessor agreement.

Sequencing note

The 2024 American Heart Association and American Red Cross first aid guidelines describe direct pressure as the first action for life-threatening bleeding, followed by a tourniquet or wound packing where the wound location allows. This lesson teaches that first action. It is designed as the opening block ahead of the tourniquet and wound-packing lessons.

Review the Design | Section B

Objectives

Terminal learning objective

Given a simulated external-bleeding casualty, a task trainer, a training first-aid kit, and a second responder, the learner will control bleeding with direct pressure and deliver a verbal handoff, performing all critical steps on the performance checklist without instructor prompting.

Enabling learning objectives. By the end of this lesson, the learner will:
No.ObjectiveBloom's domain and levelWhere assessed
1Identify the signs of life-threatening external bleeding in a given scenario.Cognitive: UnderstandOnline
2Select the correct initial safety and help-activation actions.Cognitive: ApplyOnline, then in person
3Apply and maintain direct pressure on a task trainer in accordance with the performance checklist.Psychomotor (Simpson): guided response in practice, independent performance at assessmentIn person only
4Reassess bleeding and take corrective action when bleeding continues.Cognitive: AnalyzeOnline, then in person
5Deliver a verbal handoff that states the injury, the actions taken, and the casualty's current status.Cognitive: ApplyOnline, then in person

How each objective is built

Each objective states a condition, an observable behavior, and a standard. The verb sets the Bloom's level, and the level decides how the objective is taught and assessed.

Why the levels matter

The objectives start at Understand and climb to Analyze. None stops at recall. Objective 3 sits in the psychomotor domain, so it is taught by demonstration and assessed by observation.

Review the Design | Section D

Instructor plan

A 30-minute lesson: 5 to 7 minutes of online instruction and decisions, then 23 minutes of practical work.

Delivery schedule
TimeActivityInstructor responsibility
0 to 2 minutesIntroduce the scenarioEstablish relevance and elicit initial thinking
2 to 7 minutesOnline instruction and decisionsReview recognition and decision-making
7 to 11 minutesDemonstrationDemonstrate the skill and explain decisions
11 to 19 minutesGuided practiceObserve practice and provide specific corrective feedback
19 to 25 minutesIndividual assessmentAssess without coaching using the performance checklist
25 to 30 minutesHandoff, debrief, and remediation planningReview performance and identify next steps

Materials

  • Simulated limb or bleeding-control task trainer
  • Training dressings and gauze
  • Gloves
  • Scenario cards
  • Performance checklists, one per learner

Instructor notes

  • Every learner must have an individual opportunity to practice and to be assessed.
  • The six-minute assessment window fits about four learners per assessor, at roughly 90 seconds each. For a larger class, run assessment stations with one assessor for every four learners, or extend the block. The pilot confirms this figure.
  • Introduce the "bleeding continues" cue during practice so no learner meets it for the first time during the assessment.

Scoring rules

  1. Any critical step rated Prompted or Not demonstrated: remediation required.
  2. Otherwise, any step still Not assessed: assessment incomplete.
  3. Every step rated Independent: all criteria met.
  4. All critical steps Independent with a required step Prompted or Not demonstrated: additional practice required.

Review the Design | Section F

Remediation

A missed step tells the instructor what to teach next. The learner gets focused help on that gap and then a fair second attempt.

  1. IdentifyIdentify the specific missed behavior.
  2. DiagnoseDetermine whether the gap concerns knowledge, decision-making, communication, or physical performance.
  3. Re-teachProvide focused explanation or demonstration.
  4. PracticeAllow additional coached practice.
  5. ReassessReassess individually using an equivalent scenario.
  6. DocumentDocument the outcome and any remaining need through METC's approved process.

Example

A learner applies direct pressure correctly but does not respond when the instructor says bleeding is continuing. Remediation focuses on recognizing and acting on that cue. The learner does not repeat the entire lesson.

Review the Design | Section G

Evaluation, retention, and transfer

The lesson is evaluated with Kirkpatrick's four levels. Each measure below answers one question about whether the training worked.

Evaluation plan by Kirkpatrick level
LevelMeasureQuestion it answers
1. ReactionEnd-of-lesson learner surveyDid learners find the lesson relevant and feel ready to act?
2. LearningFirst-attempt question responsesWhich concepts or decisions are misunderstood?
2. LearningFirst-attempt observed performanceWhich behaviors require prompting or correction?
2. LearningRemediation outcomesDoes the targeted support address the identified gap?
2. LearningDelayed reassessmentIs performance retained after initial instruction?
3. BehaviorSupervised performance evidenceDoes the learning transfer to clinical or field training?
4. ResultsOutcome measure set with METCWhat result does METC expect this training to improve?

Quality checks on the lesson itself

  • Assessor comparison. Do qualified assessors rate the same performance the same way?
  • Instructor feedback. Are the directions, materials, timing, and criteria usable?

How far this plan reaches

Levels 1 and 2 are measured inside the lesson. Level 3 needs access to later supervised training. Level 4 belongs to METC, so the measure is chosen with them.

Retention and transfer

Passing the simulation shows the learner can perform under the conditions that were assessed. It does not, by itself, establish consistent performance on the job. The follow-up plan includes a delayed reassessment and observation during supervised clinical or field training.

Second simulation scenario: the motor pool

Weeks later, a wrench slips in the motor pool. A trainee backs away from the engine bay holding her forearm, and blood is already on the concrete. The aid bag is in another vehicle. The only other person nearby has never done this and is waiting for you to say something.

Partway through, the assessor says, "Bleeding is continuing."

Purpose of the second scenario

To find out whether the learner can apply the response sequence in a new setting, with supplies in a different place and a helper who needs direction.

Review the Design | Section I

How this lesson is built

If I were handing this lesson to an instructor team, this is the one page I would walk them through. Five principles shaped it.

1. Start with the task and work backward

The lesson began with one question: what does a new trainee have to do when someone in front of them is bleeding? Every objective, activity, and checklist step traces back to that task. Content that did not support it was cut.

2. Adults learn from a problem they care about (Knowles)

Adult learners want to know why something matters, and they learn best when instruction is built around a real problem. So the lesson opens with Reyes bleeding at 0540 and asks for a decision before it teaches anything. The learner feels the need first, and the content answers it.

3. Objectives climb Bloom's taxonomy

Each objective is written at a specific Bloom's level, and the level decides how it is taught and assessed.

Bloom's levelIn this lessonAssessed by
UnderstandTell life-threatening bleeding from a minor injuryOnline question
ApplyChoose the first actions and deliver the handoffOnline decision, then observation
AnalyzeNotice that bleeding continues and change courseOnline decision, then observation
Psychomotor domainApply and hold direct pressureObservation only

This is why the lesson is blended. A screen can assess the cognitive levels. It cannot see a learner's hands. Miller's pyramid for clinical training makes the same point: knows and knows how can be tested in writing, shows how has to be observed, and does is confirmed on the job.

4. Skill comes from practice with feedback (Kolb, deliberate practice)

Learners watch the skill, try it, get corrected, and try again before anyone scores them. The debrief asks them to explain their reasoning, which is the reflection step in Kolb's cycle. Research supports the investment. In one randomized trial (Goralnick et al., JAMA Surgery, 2018), 88% of people who took an in-person bleeding control course applied a tourniquet correctly, compared with about 20% of those given flashcards. Only 54.5% could still do it 3 to 9 months later, which is why this lesson plans a delayed reassessment.

5. Evaluate with Kirkpatrick's four levels

Bloom's tells me what to teach and how to test it. Kirkpatrick tells me whether the training worked.

  • Level 1, Reaction. A short learner survey.
  • Level 2, Learning. First-attempt scores online and on the checklist.
  • Level 3, Behavior. Observation in later supervised training.
  • Level 4, Results. An outcome measure chosen with METC.

The lesson measures Levels 1 and 2 on its own. Levels 3 and 4 are planned with METC, because they depend on what happens after the classroom.
